editorial_policy.sensor_rule: The pianist reports the symptom and judges the result. This library never infers correctness from audio.
editorial_policy.advice_rule: Methods are suggestions, not diagnoses or mandatory plans. The pianist may override any suggestion.
editorial_policy.dose_rule: Numeric doses are conservative, user-adjustable operational defaults unless a source note says otherwise; they are not research-proven universal thresholds.
editorial_policy.safety_rule: Pain, weakness, swelling, pins and needles, unusual fatigue, lost dexterity, or reduced range of movement stops the drill and routes to qualified health advice.

routes.label: Fast run is uneven or fingers stumble
Wrong notes appear when the passage speeds up
Leap or jump misses its landing
Notes are learned but still slow or hunted
Memory slips or only works from the beginning
Melody is buried or voicing is flat
Trill or ornament is lumpy or locks up
Rhythm is wrong or the beat disappears
Pain, numbness, weakness, or loss of movement

methods.name: Controlled slow practice
methods.method: Choose a tempo where the selected passage can be played without searching. Keep one musical goal, such as even pulse or deliberate fingering, and let the pianist supply each verdict.
methods.dose: Use a short cell for 3-5 self-judged secure repetitions; if searching continues, reduce the tempo or the cell size.
methods.watch_for: Slow practice is not useful when attention drifts or the same error is repeated without a changed plan.

methods.name: Alternating long-short rhythms
methods.method: Transform even note pairs into long-short, then short-long, before returning to the written rhythm. The variation exposes transitions that disappear in a straight run.
methods.dose: Play each rhythm 3 controlled times, then test the written rhythm once.
methods.watch_for: The short note must stay placed rather than becoming a scramble; reduce tempo if control disappears.

methods.name: Shifted rhythmic grouping
methods.method: Regroup a continuous line in twos, threes, then fours, moving the perceived start of each group. Restore the score's accents after the exercise.
methods.dose: Use 2-3 repetitions per grouping, then one normal-rhythm check.
methods.watch_for: Temporary exercise accents must not leak into the final phrasing.

methods.name: Detached articulation check
methods.method: Play a short passage lightly detached to clarify individual releases, then immediately restore the written articulation.
methods.dose: Use 2-3 brief repetitions before a legato transfer check.
methods.watch_for: Avoid forceful lifting or extra tension; detached does not mean loud or rigid.

methods.name: Smallest failing cell
methods.method: Reduce the task to the smallest musical cell that still contains the problem, practice that cell, then reconnect it to its neighbors.
methods.dose: Aim for 3-5 secure cell repetitions before practicing both joins.
methods.watch_for: A cell practiced without its entry and exit can become reliable in isolation but fail in context.

methods.name: Forward linking
methods.method: Once one cell is secure, add the next cell and practice the join before treating both as one longer unit.
methods.dose: Practice each new join 3 secure times before extending again.
methods.watch_for: Do not lengthen the chain if the seam still causes a hesitation.

methods.name: Backward linking
methods.method: Begin with the final cell, then add one earlier cell at a time so every repetition travels toward material already recalled.
methods.dose: Use 2-3 secure repetitions per added cell.
methods.watch_for: Keep musical phrase boundaries visible; mechanical fragments are a temporary learning device.

methods.name: One-hand isolation
methods.method: Isolate the hand whose notes, fingering, or rhythm are uncertain, then recombine quickly at a lower tempo. Use isolation to diagnose and simplify, not as proof that hands together is solved.
methods.dose: Use 2-3 deliberate repetitions with the uncertain hand, then test a short hands-together cell.
methods.watch_for: Long one-hand work can avoid the actual coordination problem; return to the combined task promptly.

methods.name: Additive coordination
methods.method: Play the first coordinated attack or beat, stop, then add one beat at a time while preserving the shared vertical landmarks.
methods.dose: Add one beat after 2-3 secure repetitions of the current span.
methods.watch_for: If the same added beat fails, isolate the transition into that beat rather than restarting a longer span.

methods.name: Block the hand shape
methods.method: Temporarily play the destination notes together as a quiet chord to identify the hand shape, then restore the written sequence or leap.
methods.dose: Alternate 3-5 blocked shapes with 3 written versions.
methods.watch_for: Do not force a wide grip or hold the shape rigidly; the goal is orientation, not stretching.

methods.name: Silent landing rehearsal
methods.method: Move from the takeoff to the destination and hover or touch silently before playing the landing. Rehearse the route without judging the sound.
methods.dose: Use 5 silent landings followed by 3 played landings.
methods.watch_for: Keep the travel easy and the landing released; repeated tension defeats the purpose.

methods.name: Look before the leap
methods.method: Move the gaze to the destination before moving the hand, then execute the leap without looking back at the takeoff.
methods.dose: Use 5 deliberate gaze-first trials, then test the phrase in context.
methods.watch_for: Choose a precise key or keyboard landmark, not a vague area.

methods.name: Small-step tempo ladder
methods.method: Begin below the current ceiling. After the pianist reports a stable run, raise tempo by a small step; after instability, return to the last controlled rung.
methods.dose: CodaKiller default: 3 self-judged clean repetitions, then +2 to +4 bpm; the user may change both values.
methods.watch_for: The gate is a tracking aid, not a scientific threshold; stop laddering when attention, ease, or musical control declines.

methods.name: Isolate the tempo bottleneck
methods.method: Find the smallest transition that sets the ceiling for the larger passage and work on that transition before another full run.
methods.dose: Spend one short block on the bottleneck, then retest the surrounding phrase once or twice.
methods.watch_for: Repeated full runs can hide the actual limiting transition and add fatigue.

methods.name: Name the pattern
methods.method: Give the cell a concrete structural label, such as scale fragment, inversion, sequence, or repeated grip, and use that label as a retrieval cue.
methods.dose: Name the cell once, play it 3-5 times, then attempt one cold start from it.
methods.watch_for: A label helps only if it accurately describes what the hands and harmony are doing.

methods.name: Harmonic skeleton
methods.method: Reduce the passage to bass notes, chord functions, or major harmonic arrivals, then rebuild the surface around that map.
methods.dose: Speak or play the skeleton once, then reconstruct 2-3 short spans from it.
methods.watch_for: Do not invent an overconfident analysis; use simpler bass and harmony landmarks when the function is ambiguous.

methods.name: Cold-start anchors
methods.method: Choose structural and expressive landmarks throughout the piece and practice beginning from each without a run-up.
methods.dose: Select 4-6 anchors and make one cold start from each; revisit weak anchors later or the next day.
methods.watch_for: An anchor is not secure if it needs the preceding phrase to trigger it.

methods.name: Interleave weak spots
methods.method: Rotate among a small set of already-understood spots instead of finishing a long block on one before touching the next.
methods.dose: Rotate 3 spots for 2-3 repetitions each, then test each after a delay.
methods.watch_for: Interleaving can make practice feel worse and is not ideal for a cell that has not yet been decoded; the direct music evidence is promising but limited.

methods.name: Shape the melody alone
methods.method: Play or sing the melodic voice alone with its intended direction before restoring the accompaniment.
methods.dose: Shape 2-3 melody-only passes, then test the full texture.
methods.watch_for: The isolated line should keep its phrase and timing; it is not merely a note check.

methods.name: Exaggerated dynamic layers
methods.method: Temporarily exaggerate the dynamic difference between the intended leading voice and accompaniment, then reduce the contrast to the musical result wanted.
methods.dose: Use 3 exaggerated trials and 2 normalized trials.
methods.watch_for: Do not create the melody by stiffening or striking; listen for the layer rather than forcing it.

methods.name: Composite polyrhythm
methods.method: Write, speak, or tap the merged order of attacks, mark shared downbeats, then assign the two streams back to the hands.
methods.dose: Tap the composite 5 times, each stream 3 times, then combine at a controlled tempo.
methods.watch_for: A mnemonic is only a bridge; verify the actual score's subdivision and note placement.

methods.name: Rhythmic trill variants
methods.method: Practice a short alternation with deliberately changed rhythms, then return to a light, even trill.
methods.dose: Use 2-3 trials of each variant, followed by one even trill.
methods.watch_for: Stop the trial if the forearm hardens, speed drops sharply, or discomfort appears.

methods.name: Expand a relaxed ornament
methods.method: Begin with a very short, easy alternation and add notes only while the motion remains released and even.
methods.dose: Try 2, 4, 6, then 8 notes, returning to the last easy length when control changes.
methods.watch_for: Length and speed are secondary to ease; never continue through pain or numbness.

methods.name: Clarify without pedal
methods.method: Remove pedal to hear voicing, releases, and harmonic joins clearly, then add only the pedal needed for the desired sound.
methods.dose: Use 1-2 no-pedal diagnostic passes, then 2 slow passes with pedal.
methods.watch_for: No-pedal work is diagnostic; do not force finger legato where the score or hand cannot support it comfortably.

methods.name: After-attack pedal change
methods.method: For legato pedaling, release and retake the pedal after the new harmony sounds, adjusting the timing by ear and by the instrument's resonance.
methods.dose: Isolate 3-5 harmony changes, then test the phrase once.
methods.watch_for: Pedal timing is acoustic and context-dependent; a fixed timing rule cannot replace listening.

methods.name: Speak the smallest pulse
methods.method: Count or speak the smallest relevant subdivision through notes and rests, then play while retaining that grid internally.
methods.dose: Count once away from the keys, play 2-3 times with the subdivision, then once without speaking.
methods.watch_for: Use a subdivision that clarifies the disputed rhythm; over-counting can make a fluent passage rigid.

methods.name: Remove pitch from the rhythm
methods.method: Clap, tap, or speak the rhythm without playing pitches, then restore the notes after the durations and rests are clear.
methods.dose: Make 3 accurate rhythm-only passes, then 2 played transfers.
methods.watch_for: Preserve the meter and rests; tapping a stream of attacks without the beat does not solve the rhythm.

methods.name: Safety stop and reset
methods.method: Stop the current drill. If the issue is ordinary effort without symptoms, rest and reassess load and ease. Pain, weakness, swelling, pins and needles, unusual fatigue, reduced dexterity, or reduced movement requires qualified health advice rather than more repetitions.
methods.dose: No repetition dose is prescribed for pain or neurological symptoms.
methods.watch_for: Do not mask symptoms, play through pain, or let the app diagnose an injury.

psychology_principles.title: Practice quality before elapsed time
psychology_principles.practice: State one observable problem, choose one response, and check whether the response changed the next attempt. Change the task when it did not.
psychology_principles.dose: Use one question-method-check cycle per short block rather than measuring success by minutes alone.
psychology_principles.watch_for: The supporting piano study observed 17 advanced pianists on one short passage; it identifies useful behavior patterns, not a universal formula.
psychology_principles.evidence_note: Primary observational research in advanced pianists linked the quality and timing of corrective practice behaviors, rather than practice amount alone, with next-day retention performance.

psychology_principles.title: Rotate material when long-term retention is the goal
triggers: one spot feels good only immediately after drilling
psychology_principles.practice: Alternate among a few already-decoded passages and retest them after another task has intervened.
psychology_principles.dose: Rotate 2-4 passages in short blocks and include a delayed check.
psychology_principles.watch_for: A music-specific study found a retention advantage in only ten advanced clarinetists; interleaving can impair immediate fluency and should not replace initial decoding.
psychology_principles.evidence_note: A small primary music study found better one-day retention after interleaved than blocked schedules, while broader contextual-interference effects are task-dependent.

psychology_principles.title: Revisit across time, but do not promise a spacing effect
psychology_principles.practice: Schedule a later cold check instead of treating immediate repetition as proof of retention.
psychology_principles.dose: Retest after another passage and again on a later day when the schedule allows.
psychology_principles.watch_for: A controlled novice-piano experiment found no benefit from 1-15 minute lags on its tasks, so the app must not claim that every spacing interval improves piano learning.
psychology_principles.evidence_note: Direct piano evidence is mixed: short within-session lags did not improve measured outcomes in one randomized study; later-day retrieval remains a useful test rather than a guaranteed treatment.

psychology_principles.title: Build more than motor-sequence memory
triggers: can only start at the beginning
psychology_principles.practice: Use structural analysis and planned performance cues, then retrieve from multiple cold-start locations without a run-up.
psychology_principles.dose: Test several starts and explain the structure away from the keyboard.
psychology_principles.watch_for: The central source is an intensive case study of one concert pianist; use it as an expert model, not population-level proof.
psychology_principles.evidence_note: Longitudinal case research documented how formal structure and performance cues served as retrieval organization in expert piano memorization.

psychology_principles.title: Combine mental and physical rehearsal
psychology_principles.practice: Study the score, imagine sound and movement, and mentally traverse a short passage; verify the result at the instrument later.
psychology_principles.dose: Use short, specific mental passes interleaved with physical verification.
psychology_principles.watch_for: Mental practice is not a substitute for physical feedback on unfamiliar technique; studies are small and use different instruments and protocols.
psychology_principles.evidence_note: Primary studies in pianists and classical guitarists found that structured mental rehearsal can support memorization, especially when combined with physical practice.

psychology_principles.title: Let consolidation happen and retest
psychology_principles.practice: End with a controlled attempt, sleep normally, and retest before re-drilling the next day.
psychology_principles.dose: Record the end-of-day state and one next-day cold result.
psychology_principles.watch_for: Sleep studies use brief laboratory keyboard sequences; they do not prove that every repertoire problem improves overnight.
psychology_principles.evidence_note: Primary keyboard-sequence studies observed offline gains after sleep, supporting next-day retest as measurement rather than extra same-night grinding.

psychology_principles.title: Practice the performance situation
psychology_principles.practice: Run the prepared excerpt under progressively more realistic observation: recording, one trusted listener, then a small audience. Debrief constructively and repeat only while healthy.
psychology_principles.dose: Use occasional complete simulations, not constant high-pressure runs.
psychology_principles.watch_for: A primary study used 18 string players and three same-day performances; exposure may not fit severe anxiety and is not a replacement for clinical care.
psychology_principles.evidence_note: Repeated live performance in a small musician sample reduced heart rate, self-reported anxiety, restlessness, and rated errors across three exposures.

psychology_principles.title: Aim attention at sound and communication in performance
psychology_principles.practice: During a well-learned performance run, choose an external musical target such as phrase destination, projected sound, or communication to the listener.
psychology_principles.dose: Compare one external-focus run with the normal approach and keep it only if it helps.
psychology_principles.watch_for: One experiment favored external focus, but a later systematic review found no consistent overall winner across music studies; individualize the cue.
psychology_principles.evidence_note: Two experiments with skilled musicians found better expert ratings under external-focus instructions, while the wider evidence base remains heterogeneous.

psychology_principles.title: Unload pre-performance worry onto paper
psychology_principles.practice: Before a performance simulation, write privately for ten minutes about the thoughts and feelings occupying attention, then perform without trying to solve the writing.
psychology_principles.dose: One ten-minute trial before a simulation; keep only if it is useful.
psychology_principles.watch_for: The piano study was small and benefits were strongest among highly anxious participants; this is not therapy or a guaranteed anxiety treatment.
psychology_principles.evidence_note: A randomized expressive-writing study with college piano students reported reductions in anxiety and performance errors for highly anxious participants.

psychology_principles.title: Replace judgment with one task cue
psychology_principles.practice: Replace evaluative commentary with one brief neutral cue tied to the next action, such as 'breathe,' 'bass arrival,' or 'sing the line.'
psychology_principles.dose: Choose one cue before the run; do not narrate continuously while playing.
psychology_principles.watch_for: Music-specific evidence here is preliminary and self-talk effects vary by task; frequent internal commentary can itself distract.
psychology_principles.evidence_note: In a small piano experiment, anxious participants' post-intervention self-talk shifted from harsh evaluation toward sparse instructional content; general causal evidence comes mostly from sport, so the library stays cautious.

sources.title: On Piano Playing: Motion, Sound, and Expression
sources.claim_scope: Piano movement patterns, scales and arpeggios, articulation, pedaling, memorization, and conscious practice.
sources.limitations: Authoritative pedagogy, not a controlled trial; exact operational doses in this library are editorial defaults.

sources.title: Piano Technique
sources.claim_scope: Conscious practice, score study, memory, rhythm, dynamics, and pedal in piano playing.
sources.limitations: Authoritative pedagogy, not a controlled trial; some recommendations reflect its historical context.

sources.title: Mastering Piano Technique: A Guide for Students, Teachers and Performers
sources.claim_scope: Anatomically informed piano movement, coordination, articulation, and technical exercises.
sources.limitations: Authoritative pedagogy, not clinical or controlled evidence.

sources.title: The Art of Piano Playing
sources.claim_scope: Piano sound, rhythm, technique, artistic conception, voicing, and interpretation.
sources.limitations: Authoritative pedagogy and artistic reflection, not experimental evidence.

sources.title: It's Not How Much; It's How: Characteristics of Practice Behavior and Retention of Performance Skills
sources.venue: Journal of Research in Music Education 56(4), 310-321
sources.claim_scope: Observed practice behaviors and next-day retention in 17 advanced pianists learning a short difficult passage.
sources.limitations: Small observational study of one task; does not establish universal causal doses.

sources.title: Optimizing Music Learning: Exploring How Blocked and Interleaved Practice Schedules Affect Advanced Performance
sources.claim_scope: Blocked versus interleaved practice and one-day retention in ten advanced clarinetists.
sources.limitations: Very small sample, one instrument, and short retention interval.

sources.title: Lack of Spacing Effects During Piano Learning
sources.claim_scope: Randomized comparison of 0-15 minute lags in novice piano-sequence and melody learning.
sources.limitations: Novices, short tasks, short lags, and a five-minute final retention interval; found no spacing advantage.

sources.title: Practicing Perfection: Piano Performance as Expert Memory
sources.claim_scope: Longitudinal case study of formal structure, performance cues, and retrieval practice in one concert pianist.
sources.limitations: Single expert case; useful mechanism evidence but not population-level effect estimation.

sources.title: Mental Practice in Music Memorization: An Ecological-Empirical Study
sources.claim_scope: Mental versus physical memorization strategies in sixteen pianists.
sources.limitations: Small sample and individualized strategies; does not prescribe a universal imagery protocol.

sources.title: The Effect of Mental Practice on Music Memorization
sources.claim_scope: One-week physical-plus-mental versus physical practice protocol in classical guitarists, including delayed retention.
sources.limitations: Different instrument and a specific memorization protocol; not evidence that mental practice replaces physical feedback.

sources.title: Effects of Sleep on Performance of a Keyboard Melody
sources.venue: Journal of Research in Music Education 54(3), 257-269
sources.claim_scope: Sleep-related consolidation in performance of a brief keyboard melody.
sources.limitations: Brief laboratory task; transfer to complex repertoire is uncertain.

sources.title: Practice with Sleep Makes Perfect: Sleep-Dependent Motor Skill Learning
sources.claim_scope: Sleep and offline gains in a sequential finger-tapping task.
sources.limitations: Non-musical laboratory task; repertoire learning is substantially more complex.

sources.title: Repeated Stage Exposure Reduces Music Performance Anxiety
sources.claim_scope: Three same-day live performances in eighteen string players reporting performance anxiety.
sources.limitations: Small uncontrolled repeated-exposure study; instrument group and same-day design limit generalization.

sources.title: Adopting an External Focus of Attention Enhances Musical Performance
sources.venue: Journal of Research in Music Education 66(4), 375-391
sources.claim_scope: Two experiments comparing external, internal, and usual attentional focus in skilled musicians.
sources.limitations: Later systematic review found heterogeneous and inconsistent results across the wider music literature.

sources.title: Music Performance Anxiety: Can Expressive Writing Intervention Help?
sources.claim_scope: Randomized ten-minute expressive-writing intervention in 35 college piano students.
sources.limitations: Small sample, two performance types, and strongest effects in highly anxious participants.

sources.title: Mechanisms Underlying the Self-Talk-Performance Relationship: The Effects of Motivational Self-Talk on Self-Confidence and Anxiety
sources.claim_scope: Experimental motivational self-talk training in 72 young tennis players.
sources.limitations: Sport rather than music and motivational rather than piano-specific instructional cues; used only as indirect evidence.

sources.title: Returning to Playing and Performance for Instrumental Musicians
authors: British Association for Performing Arts Medicine
sources.claim_scope: Symptom red flags, gradual playing load, and seeking performing-arts health advice.
sources.limitations: General health guidance, not individual diagnosis or treatment.

sources.title: Healthy Practice Resources
authors: British Association for Performing Arts Medicine
sources.claim_scope: Healthy instrumental practice, warm-up, physical and psychological care, and musician-specific support.
sources.limitations: General prevention guidance, not individual diagnosis or treatment.
